questions.question: What exactly is the DRY principle according to The Pragmatic Programmer, and what is the test that lets you check whether code violates it?
What is the difference between tracer bullets and prototypes, and when should you use which?
Why do the authors claim that inheritance is a tax, and which three alternatives do they propose?

questions.header: Relacyjne / multi-hop (wymaga połączenia faktów z różnych Topiców)
questions.question: How does the ETC principle connect with the other design principles in the book — decoupling, DRY, and orthogonality? Is ETC a rule or a value?
The book says that when you find a broken window in code, it is best to leave it alone until the end of the project so as not to disrupt the team's flow. Is that correct?
What are preconditions, postconditions, and class invariants in Design by Contract, and who is responsible for checking them?

questions.header: Porównanie czterech strategii (comparison, multi-chunk w jednym Topicu)
questions.question: What four strategies for dealing with events does the book describe, and how do they differ in terms of coupling and asynchronicity?
Why is crashing early better than a program continuing silently after an error is detected? How does this connect with the Catch-and-Release-is-for-Fish approach?
The book suggests that assertions should be turned off in the production version of the program, because they add overhead and slow the code down. Is that correct?
How does DRY differ from Orthogonality? Are they the same thing, or two different principles? How do they complement each other?
What is a binary chop in the context of debugging, and in which three situations does the book recommend using it?

questions.header: Porównanie modeli współbieżności (comparison, dwa sąsiednie Topics)
questions.question: How does the actor model differ from the blackboard as a way of dealing with concurrency? When should you use which?
What is programming by coincidence and why is it dangerous? What specific types of accidents do the authors list?

The book advises that at the start of a project you should gather complete requirements, write them down in a detailed document, and give the document to the client for signing, to avoid later changes. Is that correct?
What is the Pragmatic Starter Kit, and why do the authors claim that its three elements are inseparably linked? How do they connect with the rest of the book?
Why does the book claim that plain text is the best format for storing knowledge? Which three concrete benefits does it list?
When should you refactor code according to the book? Which specific situations do the authors list as signals to refactor, and what safety rules do they give?
Which two approaches to configuration does the book describe, and how do they differ? Which do the authors prefer and why?
The book says that sign your work means you should defend your code against interference from others and treat it as your own territory. Is that correct?

How does the finish-what-you-start principle from How to Balance Resources connect with Design by Contract and with Don't Outrun Your Headlights? How do these three principles jointly influence design?
Which five guidelines for investing in your knowledge portfolio does the book give, and why does it treat knowledge as an expiring asset?
Why is naming things so important according to the book? What is the Stroop effect, and how does it relate to naming in code?
How does the book advise estimating algorithm complexity using common sense, and when should you NOT optimize?
Which five basic security principles does the book list, and what specifically does it advise in each of them?
Why does the book claim that shared state is incorrect state? What solution does it propose, and what are that solution's drawbacks?

questions.header: Comparison (pipelines vs train wrecks, OO vs transformations)
questions.question: How does the transforming-programming style differ from the object-oriented approach? Why do the authors prefer pipelines, and how do pipelines differ from train wrecks?
What concrete advice about communication does the book give? How should communication be treated in the context of programming?
The book says that good-enough software means you may write careless, poorly designed code, as long as you deliver on time. Is that correct?
Why does the book claim that you should use version control always, even in one-person projects, and even for things that are not source code?

questions.header: Relational / multi-hop (jak praktyki indywidualne skalują się do zespołu)
questions.question: How do pragmatic practices for individuals translate to teams? Which of the book's principles do the authors explicitly carry over to the team level in Topic 49?
How do you configure an ingress controller and a horizontal pod autoscaler in Kubernetes for a microservices application?
What are the best practices for using the useEffect and useMemo hooks in React 18 to prevent unnecessary re-renders?
How do you implement secure authorization with JWT tokens and a refresh-token mechanism in the OAuth 2.0 protocol?
How do you secure a PostgreSQL database against SQL injection attacks using parameterized queries in SQLAlchemy?
What are the differences between git merge and git rebase, and in which situations is interactive rebase in Git discouraged within teams?
How do you configure Docker multi-stage builds to minimize the size of the production image of a Node.js application?
How do you design a GraphQL schema using DataLoader to solve the N+1 query problem in database access?
How do serverless functions in AWS Lambda work with regard to cold starts and memory limits?
According to the authors, does achieving 100% unit-test code coverage guarantee the absence of hidden bugs in a production system?
According to the book, should refactoring be planned as a separate, multi-week technical sprint in the team's calendar, once per quarter?
Do the authors recommend using deep class-inheritance hierarchies instead of composition in order to maximize code reuse?
Is the genuinely Agile approach, according to the authors, a strict adherence to Scrum ceremonies, estimation in story points, and process certification?
Do the authors advise ignoring the subconscious feeling of resistance before writing code, and forcing yourself to immediately crank out the lines?
Do the authors recommend throwing and catching exceptions as the standard mechanism for controlling the normal flow of business logic?
Do the authors advise that, before initiating any innovation in a project, you should always wait for formal approval from management and a full budget?
What do the authors mean when they write that you have agency in your professional career, and how should you react to a toxic work environment?
What is the pragmatic rule for responding to a problem when something goes wrong in a project: provide options, don't make lame excuses?
Why is reversibility of decisions so important in software architecture, and what does it mean in practice?
How do internal DSLs differ from external DSLs according to the authors, and when should you use them?
In which units of time do the authors recommend giving estimates, depending on the task's time horizon?
Why do the authors claim that every pragmatic programmer should be fluent in the command-line shell?
What does the advice to use a single editor well mean, and why is it worth mastering an editor to the level of unconditional reflexes?
Why do the authors claim that text is the universal interface of computing, and why should you master text-manipulation tools?
What is an engineering daybook, and what benefits does keeping one daily bring?
Where and how should application configuration data be stored according to the book's recommendations?
What is temporal coupling, and how should you design systems that allow tasks to run concurrently?
What does the advice to listen to your lizard brain mean, and how should a programmer react to a subconscious feeling of resistance before writing code?
How do the authors advise approaching seemingly unsolvable programming and algorithmic problems?
What are the rules of effective pair programming, and why does coding in a pair not mean looking over your colleague's shoulder?
What is the ultimate goal of creating software, and what does the principle of delighting your users mean?
